name: Lateral Ankle Sprain
summary: The outer (lateral) ankle is held by three main ligaments: the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), the calcaneofibular ligament (CFL) and the posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL). A lateral ankle sprain is a stretch or tear of these ligaments, most often the ATFL, when the foot turns inward under the body (inversion with plantar flexion), for example when landing or stepping on uneven ground.

looksLike: A rolling or twisting injury, sometimes with a pop, followed by pain and swelling over the outer ankle.
Bruising, often in the following days.
Difficulty walking or pushing off; reduced movement.
A feeling that the ankle is unstable or gives way, particularly in repeat injuries.
redFlags: Ottawa rule positive, deformity, or severe pain
Pale, cold or pulseless foot, or severe swelling with intense pain
Positive calf squeeze test or palpable gap in the Achilles
Pain above the ankle with positive squeeze test
Hot red swollen ankle with fever
Pain not improving after about 6 weeks, or recurrent swelling and catching
firstSteps: Initial approach: apply the Ottawa rules, protect and begin early graded loading.
Justifying findings: mechanism, outer ankle swelling, positive drawer or tilt, no fracture signs.
Priority: restore range, strength and balance.

assess: Apply a fracture decision rule first (Section E).
Palpate the lateral malleolus, medial malleolus, base of the 5th metatarsal, navicular, ATFL, CFL and the area above the ankle (syndesmosis).
Range of movement: dorsiflexion, plantar flexion, inversion and eversion.
Ligament tests (best 4 to 5 days after injury when pain and swelling are lower).
Strength and balance once pain allows.

blocks.text: The outer (lateral) ankle is held by three main ligaments: the **anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL)**, the **calcaneofibular ligament (CFL)** and the **posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL)**. A **lateral ankle sprain** is a stretch or tear of these ligaments, most often the ATFL, when the foot turns inward under the body (inversion with plantar flexion), for example when landing or stepping on uneven ground [Ref - to verify].

It is one of the most common sports and daily-life injuries. Many people recover well, but a share have recurrent sprains or lasting symptoms such as pain, swelling or a feeling of instability (chronic ankle instability) [Ref - to verify]. Early assessment, safe loading and exercise reduce this risk.

items: A rolling or twisting injury, sometimes with a pop, followed by pain and swelling over the outer ankle.
Bruising, often in the following days.
Difficulty walking or pushing off; reduced movement.
A feeling that the ankle is unstable or gives way, particularly in repeat injuries.

blocks.text: **Grades (clinical teaching grades, not a diagnostic standard):** mild (stretch, little swelling, can walk), moderate (partial tear, swelling and bruising, painful weight-bearing, some laxity), severe (complete tear, marked swelling, marked laxity). Treatment is guided by function, not only the grade [Ref - to verify].

rows: How did the ankle twist? Inward, outward, or a twist with the foot planted?
Lateral sprain versus syndesmosis or fracture
Did you hear a crack or pop?
Could you take four steps straight afterwards?
Where is the pain: outer ankle, above the ankle, midfoot, or the outer foot?
Any numbness, pins and needles or cold foot?
What sport or work do you need to return to?

blocks.text: E1. Ottawa ankle rules (screen for fracture before testing ligaments)

rows: Decide whether an X-ray is needed after an acute ankle or midfoot injury
Ankle X-ray series is suggested if there is pain in the malleolar zone plus
Bone tenderness at the back edge or tip of either malleolus (along the lower 6 cm), or inability to bear weight for four steps both immediately after injury and at examination
Foot X-ray series is suggested if there is pain in the midfoot zone plus
Bone tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal or at the navicular, or inability to bear weight for four steps
Any listed finding; refer for imaging
None of the findings; fracture is unlikely
Designed for adults and older children; high sensitivity but not perfect, with a low false-negative rate when used correctly [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: E2. Anterior drawer test of the ankle

rows: Sitting with the knee bent and the foot relaxed, or supine; ankle in about 10 to 20 degrees of plantar flexion
One hand holds the lower shin (tibia) still from the front; the other cups the heel from behind
Pull the heel forward while pushing the tibia backward. Compare the amount of movement and the end-feel with the other ankle
Increased forward movement of the foot, a soft end-feel, or a dimple (suction sign) over the front of the outer ankle
Similar to the other side, firm end-feel
More accurate when performed 4 to 5 days after the injury than immediately, because pain and swelling cause guarding [Ref - to verify]; comparison with the other side is essential
Pulling with the toes or foot held tense; not stabilising the tibia; testing a very painful ankle

blocks.text: E3. Talar tilt test

rows: Test the CFL (in neutral) and ATFL (in plantar flexion)
Lying or sitting; ankle in neutral for the CFL
Hold the lower shin still and tilt the heel inward (inversion stress); compare with the other side
More opening than the other side or a soft end-feel
Reliability varies; often painful in the acute phase

blocks.text: E4. Syndesmosis (high ankle sprain) tests

rows: Squeeze the shin and calf bones together at mid-calf
Pain in the area above the ankle
Sitting, knee bent to 90 degrees; stabilise the shin and rotate the foot outward
Press along the front of the syndesmosis

blocks.text: A positive result suggests a syndesmosis injury. This needs a different and longer rehabilitation and possibly imaging [Ref - to verify].
E5. Other checks

Palpate the Achilles tendon. A palpable gap or a positive Thompson test (squeezing the calf with the patient prone should plantar flex the foot; absence suggests rupture) means Achilles rupture and urgent referral. Check the peroneal tendons for pain or snapping.

rows: Bone tenderness, inability to bear weight
Pain above the ankle, positive squeeze or rotation test
5th metatarsal base avulsion or Jones fracture
Tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal
Pain behind the lateral malleolus, snapping
Persistent pain and swelling beyond about 6 weeks, catching

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Any emergency or urgent flag? **Yes:** act as in Section G.
Ottawa rules positive? **Yes:** refer for imaging.
Ottawa negative, lateral pain and swelling, and positive anterior drawer or talar tilt, particularly 4 to 5 days after injury? **Yes:** working diagnosis is lateral ankle sprain.
Positive syndesmosis tests? **Yes:** treat as a possible syndesmosis injury and seek medical review.
Otherwise: begin protected loading and exercise.

rows: Mobilization with movement (talocrural glide for dorsiflexion)
May improve dorsiflexion range and short-term function [Ref - to verify]
Weight-bearing lunge, apply a gentle posterior glide of the talus with a belt or hands, repeated pain-free

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** early protected loading and exercise. Manual therapy is optional for short-term range and comfort. Avoid forcing inversion stress through an injured ligament.

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

blocks.text: **Principle:** early functional treatment (protection with a brace or tape, early walking, and progressive exercise) gives better results than prolonged immobilisation for most sprains [Ref - to verify]. A short period of support (for example a few days up to a few weeks in more severe sprains) can be used for comfort.

rows: Ankle alphabet, pumps, gentle dorsiflexion and plantar flexion, walking with support
Walking without a limp, swelling reducing
Band eversion and inversion, calf raises, toe raises, sit-to-stand
Pain-free, strength near the other side
Single-leg stand (eyes open, then eyes closed, then on a cushion), wobble board, reach drills
Hopping, landing, cutting, figure-8 running, sport drills

blocks.text: **Return to sport criteria (example):** full pain-free range, near-normal strength, balance equal to the other side, no swelling, confidence in hopping and cutting, and passing sport-specific tests. Many athletes use tape or a brace for a period after return, which reduces recurrence in people with a history of sprains [Ref - to verify]. No fixed date is set.
**Recurrence prevention:** continuing balance and strengthening exercise lowers the risk of repeated sprains [Ref - to verify].

rows: Recommended for support and return to sport
Choose based on comfort and access [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: The older RICE rule (rest, ice, compression, elevation) is now often replaced by approaches that include protection and early optimal loading [Ref - to verify]. Avoid prolonged rest or immobilisation.

items: **Acute (first days):** screen flags and the Ottawa rules, protect, reduce swelling, begin early gentle movement and weight-bearing.
**Early rehabilitation:** restore range, begin strengthening and balance.
**Middle:** progress to hopping, landing and change of direction.
**Late:** sport-specific training with support as needed.
**If not improving or recurrent instability:** medical review for imaging and consider surgical opinion for chronic mechanical instability after failed rehabilitation [Ref - to verify].

blocks.text: **Case:** A 22-year-old basketball player rolled his right ankle 5 days ago. He walked off the court with a limp. Ottawa rules are negative (no bone tenderness, could take four steps). There is swelling and bruising over the outer ankle, tenderness over the ATFL, a positive anterior drawer with a soft end-feel, and a negative squeeze test. Neurovascular status is normal.

**Working diagnosis:** grade 2 lateral ankle sprain. **Plan:** brace support, early walking, range and strength work, balance training, graded return to hopping and cutting, tape or brace for return to sport, reassess weekly.
**Questions and answers**

items: Why test the ligaments 4 to 5 days later instead of immediately? Swelling, pain and guarding hide laxity in the first hours, so the delayed examination is more informative [Ref - to verify].
Why use the Ottawa rules first? They help decide who needs an X-ray, so fractures are not missed and unnecessary imaging is avoided.
Pain above the ankle and a positive squeeze test. What does that suggest? A syndesmosis injury, which often needs a longer recovery and medical review.
Why not rest the ankle for several weeks? Prolonged immobilisation can delay recovery. Early protected loading and exercise are generally better [Ref - to verify].
Why train balance after the swelling goes down? Proprioception and control are often reduced after a sprain and training lowers the risk of repeat injury [Ref - to verify].
**Initial approach:** apply the Ottawa rules, protect and begin early graded loading.
**Justifying findings:** mechanism, outer ankle swelling, positive drawer or tilt, no fracture signs.
**Priority:** restore range, strength and balance.
**Manual therapy:** optional adjunct.
**Exercise:** range, peroneal and calf strength, balance, hopping and sport drills.
**Modalities:** limited role; brace or tape for return.
**Tell the patient:** most sprains recover well; exercise reduces repeat sprains.
**Avoid:** prolonged rest, early return without strength and balance, ignoring syndesmosis signs.
**Measure:** swelling, dorsiflexion, strength, balance, hop tests, CAIT.
**If no improvement:** medical review.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** return criteria met and a prevention program in place.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** no fracture, syndesmosis injury or neurovascular problem.

items: **Can be tested:** whether exercise, bracing or taping reduces recurrence; accuracy of delayed examination.
**Hypotheses:** that balance training improves control after injury.
**Future questions:** the best surgical and non-surgical care for chronic instability.

blocks.text: Evidence not graded until references are verified.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Apply the Ottawa ankle rules.
Perform the anterior drawer and talar tilt tests and say when they are most informative.
Recognise syndesmosis injury and other urgent problems.
Build a staged rehabilitation plan with return criteria.
